result.summary: The chorus sing to Dionysus, who answers with an earthquake and fire at Semele's tomb and walks free from prison. A messenger describes the miraculous Bacchae on Kithaeron, but Pentheus calls out his army, until Dionysus bewitches him into agreeing to dress as a woman and spy on them.

scenes.title: Chorus sings of Dionysus
scenes.summary: With Dionysus led to prison, the chorus recall his birth, denounce Pentheus as Earth's dragon-born offspring, and call on the god to come.
scenes.stakes: The Bacchae fear Pentheus will bind them and that their god has been buried in the dark.

scenes.title: Earthquake and fire
scenes.summary: The voice of Dionysus shakes the palace and sets fire to Semele's tomb while the chorus fall to the ground.
scenes.stakes: The women fear the collapse of the palace and the god's wrath.

scenes.title: Dionysus tells of his escape
scenes.summary: Dionysus appears free and tells how Pentheus bound a bull and stabbed a phantom while the palace fell.

scenes.title: Pentheus confronts the stranger
scenes.summary: Pentheus furiously finds Dionysus free and orders the gates barred; a messenger arrives.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus's authority is mocked and his prisoner has escaped.

scenes.title: The messenger's tale
scenes.summary: The herdsman describes the women waking, working miracles, tearing cattle and routing villagers, and urges Pentheus to accept the god.
scenes.stakes: The herdsmen risk being torn apart by the women.

scenes.title: Pentheus is bewitched
scenes.summary: Pentheus calls out his army, but Dionysus takes control of his mind and persuades him to go spy on the women in disguise.
scenes.stakes: Pentheus risks war with the god and, unknowingly, his life.

scenes.title: Dionysus prays for vengeance
scenes.summary: Alone with the chorus, Dionysus says Pentheus walks into the net and prays that his reason be clouded.

alias_notes.explanation: Alternate spelling of the god's name in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Dionysus gloats that the lion walks into the net, marking Pentheus's doom.
Warning against kicking against the pricks, a proverb of futile resistance to a god.

analysis.text: Pentheus's rigid reason is overpowered as Dionysus takes control of his mind, showing the danger of denying irrational forces.
The messenger's account reflects Dionysiac ritual of maenads in the hills, including miracles of wine, milk and honey, and animal dismemberment.

legacy.text: The phrase 'kick against the pricks' appears here and later in the Acts of the Apostles, becoming a common English idiom.

fun_facts.text: The Bacchae was produced after Euripides' death in Macedon, and it won first prize in Athens.

language_notes.text: Dirce is a spring at Thebes; Acheloues is the great river-god of Greece, so 'daughter' makes the spring his offspring. The Babe is the infant Dionysus, said to have been bathed there.
Dionysus was rescued from the fire that killed his mother Semele, then sewn into Jove's thigh. This is his 'second portal' of birth.
Bromios means 'the Roaring One', a cult title of Dionysus.
'Hie me' means 'hurry'; the chorus say they still hasten to Dirce.
Pentheus descends from Echion, one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus at Thebes; hence 'child of Earth'.
The Giants, born of Earth, rose in war against the gods and were struck down by thunderbolts.
The 'golden wand' is the thyrsus, a fennel staff tipped with ivy or a pine cone, carried by Dionysus' followers.
Orpheus, legendary singer, charmed trees and beasts with his music. The Corycian Cave is on Mount Parnassus, and Olympus lies in the north.
Pierie is Pieria, near Olympus in Macedonia. The Axios and Lydias are its rivers; the 'Father-Stream' is probably the Axios.
"Io" is a ritual cry of excitement or invocation, used in Greek worship; it is not a name here.
"Chosen" means his devoted followers, the Bacchantes, the women who follow and worship Dionysus.
The "Chained Earthquake" is addressed as a spirit of the earth, held bound until the god commands it to shake the palace.
"Unveil the Lightning's eye" means reveal or kindle the lightning's flash; the "fire that sleeps" is lightning's fire lying dormant.
"Enhallowed sod" means sanctified earth: Semele's tomb was made holy by her death by lightning.
Refers to Semele's death, when Zeus appeared in his lightning and she was consumed, while carrying Dionysus.
"Damsels of the Morning Hills" addresses the chorus of Bacchae, Dionysus' female followers, who came from Asia (Mount Tmolus).
"Gyved" means shackled; a gyve is a fetter or shackle.
"Bull of Offering" means a bull kept for sacrifice; the stall is the stable where Pentheus imprisoned Dionysus.
"Hied" means hurried; "thralls" are slaves or servants; "amain" means with full force; "roof-tree" is the roof beam, meaning the house.
"Recking light of" means caring little for; "my Chosen" are his chosen followers, the Bacchae.
"But soft" is an archaic call for quiet or attention; "withal" means with it, or in addition.
"Knave" means a rascal or low fellow; "hath" is archaic "has." Pentheus uses contemptuous language for Dionysus.
"Sirrah" is a contemptuous form of address to an inferior; "show'st thou before my portals" means "do you appear before my gates."
"Set a quiet carriage to thy rage" means to bring calm bearing to his anger; "carriage" here means deportment.
Refers to Dionysus's earlier warning that a god would free him; he means himself, speaking of his own divinity in the third person.
The one who gave men the cultivated vine is Dionysus himself, god of wine, though Pentheus does not grasp this.
"Dionyse" is this translation's form of Dionysus; he speaks of himself in the third person.
"Withal" means "with it all" or "as well"; Pentheus orders every gate barred.
"He who hasteth from the mountain side" announces the messenger from Mount Cithaeron, who is about to arrive.
"Frore" is an archaic word meaning frozen or intensely cold.
"Wild White Women" refers to the Bacchae, the god's frenzied female worshippers, here dressed in pale robes.
"Scathe" means to harm or injure; Pentheus promises the messenger will not be punished for his report.
"It skills not" means "it is of no use" or "it does not help" to be angry at honesty.
"Bacchanals" are followers of Bacchus, the god of wine and ecstasy, also called Dionysus.
Bryony is a climbing plant with flowers and berries, used here as part of the worshippers' wreaths.
The thyrsus is a staff topped with a pine cone or ivy, carried by the god's followers.
Iacchos and Bromios are cult names of Dionysus; "Bromios" means "roaring" and "God of God born" recalls his birth from Zeus.
The Asopus is a river near Thebes whose plain provided the city's grain.
Dionysus is credited with giving mankind wine, the "grief-assuaging vine" that eases sorrow.
"Albeit" means although; the Leader says she fears to speak frankly to a king but will not conceal her belief.
"Dionyse" is this translation's spelling of Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstatic worship.
"Orbed targe" means a round shield; "spur the charger" means ride warhorses, i.e. the cavalry.
"Electran Gate" is one of the gates of Thebes, named for Electra; the king musters his troops there.
"Slipped thy chain" refers to the stranger's earlier escape from Pentheus' prison; Pentheus threatens to bind him again.
"Kick against the pricks" is a proverb about resisting a goad, which only hurts the resister; here, fighting a god.
Kithaeron is the mountain near Thebes where the Bacchic women worship.
"Crooked matters ... straightened" means these troubles can still be put right.
Pentheus sarcastically means he should obey his own slaves' wishes, rejecting the stranger's advice.
Pentheus suspects a "compact": a secret agreement among the stranger and the women to keep dancing on the hills.
"Fain" means gladly or eagerly; Dionysus says Pentheus would eagerly watch the women praying (worshipping) on the mountain.
"'Twould grieve me much to see them flown with wine" means he would be upset to see them drunk; "flown" means intoxicated, excited.
"'Twere vain to hide" means hiding would be useless; the women would soon track him down.
"Gird" means to wrap or bind with a belt; the robe would dress Pentheus as a woman.
The women's "mysteries" are secret Bacchic rites; uninitiated men were forbidden to witness them, and intruders risked death.
"Dionyse" is this translation's spelling of Dionysus; the disguised god speaks of himself in the third person.
Garb means clothing; Pentheus asks what outfit Dionysus will put on him for the disguise.
A tress is a long lock of hair; Pentheus is to wear a wig of long hair like a woman's.
A snood is a headband or hair-net worn by women. "The said Robe" means the robe already mentioned.
"Wouldst liefer" means "would you rather"; Dionysus asks whether he prefers to fight and shed blood.
"Place of watch" means a lookout point from which Pentheus can spy on the women unseen.
Means: it is wiser than answering anger with anger and paying for it with bitter retribution.
"Hest" is an archaic word for command.
"Serried lance" means spears packed closely together in ranks, a battle formation.
"Dionyse" is this translation's form of Dionysus; here he addresses himself as the god, speaking of his own power.
The "robe of sacrifice" foretells Pentheus's death; his mother Agave will kill him in the frenzy, so her "gift" is the deadly outcome.

context_notes.text: Dionysus, disguised as a Lydian stranger and priest of the god, has let Pentheus arrest him. His wand is taken and his hair cut.
Nysa is the legendary mountain where Dionysus was raised by nymphs; its location was variously placed in the east.
Maenads are the god's frenzied female worshippers; the chorus picture them following him westward from Asia to Greece.
Dionysus, god of wine and ecstasy, is the son of Zeus and the mortal Semele. Pentheus, king of Thebes, has rejected his divinity.
Pentheus is king of Thebes and Dionysus' opponent. He has had the disguised god imprisoned in his palace.
Dionysus emerges unbound, showing that the imprisonment has failed and that Pentheus cannot control him.
Pentheus' "mother's tomb" is Semele's, Dionysus' mother, killed by Jove's lightning; its flame honors her, and Dionysus is the "Lord" whose arrival shakes the house.
Dionysus is a god of illusion and transformation; here he tricks Pentheus with a phantom image of himself.
Dionysus, disguised as a Lydian stranger, was imprisoned by Pentheus, king of Thebes, but escaped by miracle.
The Messenger comes from Mount Cithaeron, where the Theban women have gone to worship Dionysus in ecstasy.
Autonoe, Ino and Agave are sisters, daughters of Cadmus. Agave is Pentheus's mother, so the revelers include his own family.
Pentheus had accused the women of drunken revelry and lust on the mountain; the herdsman says they are chaste and peaceful.
Fawn-skins and snakes were typical Bacchic dress; snakes were sacred to the god's rites.
Hysiae and Erythrae are villages on the slopes of Kithaeron, near Thebes.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, is Dionysus' cousin and denies the god's divinity, so he sees the Bacchic frenzy as rebellion.
Dionysus is disguised as a mortal stranger, so Pentheus does not know he is speaking to the god.
Thebes was famously wealthy, so offering all its gold shows how irrationally strong Pentheus's desire has become.
Dionysus is the god of wine and ecstasy; his female followers, the Bacchae, worship him in the mountains.
The fawn-skin and the wand (thyrsus, a staff tipped with ivy or a pine cone) are the standard costume of Bacchic worshippers.
Bacchanals are the women worshippers of Bacchus (Dionysus), who have left Thebes for the mountain.
Pentheus is king of Thebes and has threatened the Bacchae; to be shamed in women's dress is Dionysus's punishment.

literary_notes.text: The chorus address the spring Dirce directly, as though the water were a person able to hear and remember.
The question asserts rather than asks: Pentheus is portrayed as a monstrous, god-fighting Giant.
Pentheus thinks he has bound the god's priest, but the audience knows the prisoner is Dionysus, so the chorus's fear is misplaced.
'Winding, winding' and the flowing river catalogue give the verse a dancing, processional rhythm that mimics the god's approach.
The god addresses the Earthquake as if it were a living spirit, commanding it to wake and obey.
The question about Pentheus' hall collapsing anticipates the ruin of his house and his own destruction.
Lightning has an "eye" to unveil, and fire "sleeps" until awakened, treating natural forces as obedient beings.
The flame at the tomb recalls Semele's death, linking the god's present power to his violent birth and his mother's vindication.
Pentheus believes he has bound the god, yet he has bound a bull; the captor is the one deceived.
The picture of Pentheus stabbing empty air makes his rage look futile and absurd.
Wisdom is given a calm temper, portraying divine order as steady and unshaken, in contrast to Pentheus' fury.
The audience knows the stranger is Dionysus, so his talk of a liberator is a veiled reference to himself.
Dionysus mocks the futility of barring gates against a god who can leap any wall.
Dionysus turns Pentheus's insult back on him, claiming his wit is sharp exactly where it matters.
The sleeping women are compared to wild creatures at ease in the forest, linking them with nature.
Water springing from rock, wine, milk and honey show the god's miraculous bounty in vivid sensory detail.
The graphic violence of cattle torn apart, with blood raining from the pines, shows the women's superhuman power.
The women sweep on like birds borne by their own speed, stressing their inhuman swiftness.
Love is imagined as a being who could be slain, tying the god's survival to all joy in the world.
The frenzy is compared to a smothered fire that suddenly bursts out, conveying Pentheus' sense of hidden, spreading danger.
The audience knows the speaker is Dionysus himself, so his warning about defying the god carries a hidden threat.
The offer to lead the women hints at the deception to come, in which Pentheus himself will be led to them.
The audience knows Dionysus is controlling Pentheus's mind, while Pentheus believes these desires are his own.
Dionysus points out the contradiction: Pentheus craves a sight he says would grieve him, showing his reason is already failing.
Pentheus praises the stranger's cunning, unaware that the cunning is leading him to destruction.
Dionysus nearly reveals himself, naming the god as his prompter while Pentheus fails to understand.
Pentheus fears the Bacchae will triumph over him while Dionysus, whom he trusts as guide, is already leading him to ruin.
Pentheus is the lion and his fate a hunter's net, picturing a proud king as prey walking into a trap.
Dionysus calls himself fearful yet gentle to man, an ironic closing contrast as he prepares a brutal vengeance.
